summary: Defines the cid: and mid: URL schemes, which let one refer to messages and body parts of messages, such as an HTML part pointing to an image in the same multipart message.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines two web address schemes for email. A cid: address names one part of a message, such as an image that the HTML in the same message shows. A mid: address names a whole message, or one part of it.

questions: embed image in email with content-id
how to reference an image in an email body
subtitle: Two web address schemes for pointing at an email message or one of its parts.

tldr.problem: Email that carries a web page and its images needs a way for the HTML to refer to the images inside the same message, and news readers need a way to refer to a message by its Message-ID.
tldr.mechanism: The cid scheme wraps a Content-ID address and names one body part of a message. The mid scheme wraps a Message-ID address, with an optional Content-ID after a slash, and names a whole message or a part of it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2392 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1998 that obsoletes RFC 2111 and has not itself been obsoleted. It only refers to things, so it discloses no more than the Message-ID and Content-ID headers it wraps.

today: RFC 2392 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1998. It obsoletes RFC 2111 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the definition of the cid: and mid: URL schemes.

sections.title: Why These Two Schemes Exist
sections.content:
Using MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) inside email to carry a web page and the images that go with it needs a way for the HTML to refer to those images. That is what the Content-ID URL, the cid: scheme, is for.

News readers have the same kind of problem in reverse: they use Message-IDs to link related messages together. The Message-ID URL, the mid: scheme, gives a way to refer to such a message as a resource.

Both schemes provide identifiers. The mid scheme uses part or all of the message-id of an email message to name one message. The cid scheme names one body part of a message, and its use is generally limited to references to other body parts in the same message. The mid scheme can also name a specific body part within a named message, by including the content-ID's address.
sections.plainLanguage: Email can carry a web page and the images it shows. The cid: scheme lets the page's HTML point at those images. The mid: scheme lets a news reader point at a message by its identifier.

sections.title: Body Part and MIME Entity
sections.content: The document uses two terms interchangeably. "Body part" and "MIME entity" both mean the headers and body of a MIME message, whether that message is the whole message or one of the body parts contained in a Multipart message. The note is there so that a reader does not read "body part" as the content alone and leave the headers out.
sections.plainLanguage: Two words mean the same thing here. "Body part" and "MIME entity" both mean the headers and content of a message, or of one piece of a message that holds several pieces.

sections.title: The Syntax of cid and mid URLs
sections.content:
RFC 1738 reserves the "mid" and "cid" schemes for Message-ID and Content-ID, and this document defines the syntax of both. Because they use the same syntactic elements, they are presented together. Each carries an addr-spec, the address form of RFC 822, with URL encoding applied to it. A cid URL is the scheme name, a colon and a Content-ID. A mid URL is the scheme name, a colon, a Message-ID and, optionally, a slash and a Content-ID.

In Internet mail messages, the address in a Content-ID or Message-ID header is enclosed in angle brackets. Because that address may contain characters that are not allowed within a URL, any such character, including the "/" that is reserved within the "mid" scheme, must be hex-encoded with the %hh escape mechanism described in RFC 1738.
sections.plainLanguage: Both schemes wrap an address in the same way. A cid: address holds a Content-ID, and a mid: address holds a Message-ID and, after a slash, an optional Content-ID. Characters a web address cannot carry are written as %hh codes.

sections.title: Turning a cid URL into a Content-ID Header
sections.content:
A mid URL that carries only a Message-ID names an entire message. With the Content-ID appended, it names a body part within a message, as does a cid URL. The Content-ID of a MIME body part is required to be globally unique. However, in many systems that store messages, body parts are not indexed independently of their context, the message they belong to. The long form of the mid URL was designed to supply that context, so that such systems can interoperate.

To turn a cid URL into the matching Content-ID header, remove the cid: prefix, convert each %-encoded character to the equivalent US-ASCII character, and enclose what remains in a pair of angle brackets. For example, cid:foo4%25foo1@bar.net corresponds to Content-ID: <foo4%25foo1@bar.net>. Reversing the process, converting URL special characters to their % encodings, produces the original cid URL.

An implementation that conforms to this specification is required to support the long form of the mid URL, the message-id and content-id pair. It may choose to, but need not, use the uniqueness of a Content-ID to interpret a cid URL as naming any body part within the message store. In limited circumstances, for example within a multipart/alternate entity, a single message can contain several body parts that have the same Content-ID. That happens when identical data can be reached by different methods, and a conforming implementation must then use the rules of the containing MIME entity to select the body part meant.
sections.plainLanguage: To find the part a cid: address names, drop the prefix, turn each %hh code back into its character, and put the rest in angle brackets. That gives the exact Content-ID header to look for.

sections.title: Two Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example is a message whose body parts sit inside a Multipart/Related entity. The first part is HTML, and its IMG tag points at the image in the second part with a cid URL, cid:foo4*foo1@bar.net. The second part carries the matching Content-ID header, <foo4*foo1@bar.net>, and holds an image in base64 encoding.

The second example is a plain HTML message that points at another message with a mid URL in the long form, mid:960830.1639@XIson.com/partA.960830.1639@XIson.com. The document notes that it points to another message, hopefully still in the recipient's message store.
sections.plainLanguage: The first example is a message that carries an HTML page and an image. The page points at the image with a cid: address. The second example points from one message to another message in the reader's store.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The URLs defined here provide an addressing or referencing mechanism. Their values disclose no more about the originator's environment than the corresponding Message-ID and Content-ID values do. Where concern exists about such disclosures, the originator of a message using mid and cid URLs must take precautions to insure that confidential information is not disclosed. Those precautions should already be in place to handle existing mail use of the Message-ID and Content-ID.
sections.plainLanguage: These schemes only point at things. They reveal no more about the sender than the Message-ID and Content-ID headers already do, so the same care about those headers is enough.

sections.title: Where the Idea Came From
sections.content:
The original concept of "mid" and "cid" URLs was part of Tim Berners-Lee's original vision of the World Wide Web. The ideas and the design benefited greatly from discussions with Harald Alvestrand, Dan Connolly, Roy Fielding, Larry Masinter, Jacob Palme and others in the MHTML working group.

This document obsoletes RFC 2111. It clarifies the example on page 3 that converts a cid URL to a Content-ID, so that the example now uses a cid URL instead of a mid URL. It also corrects the example messages so that their Content-IDs use angle brackets, and adds a Message-ID header to the second example.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea came from Tim Berners-Lee's original plan for the web. People in the MHTML working group, including Harald Alvestrand, Dan Connolly, Roy Fielding, Larry Masinter and Jacob Palme, worked out the details.

viz.caption: THE SYNTAX GIVEN IN RFC 2392 SECTION 2

data.title: URL syntax
data.code:
content-id    = url-addr-spec

message-id    = url-addr-spec

url-addr-spec = addr-spec  ; URL encoding of RFC 822 addr-spec

cid-url       = "cid" ":" content-id

mid-url       = "mid" ":" message-id [ "/" content-id ]

cells: One body part, usually in the same message
A Message-ID address, optionally followed by / and a Content-ID
A whole message, or one part of it
